concepts.name: The four steps of a system design interview

questions.prompt: In the System Design Primer's approach, what is the first step of a system design interview?

choices.text: Sketch the main components and how they connect
Choose the database
Outline use cases, constraints and assumptions
Decide how to shard the data

questions.explanation: The primer's steps are: 1) outline use cases, constraints and assumptions; 2) create a high-level design; 3) design the core components; 4) scale the design. Scoping first stops you from designing the wrong system. The interview is open-ended and you are expected to lead it.

questions.prompt: Which question belongs to step 1 of the primer's approach?

choices.text: "What is the expected read to write ratio?"
"Should we shard the users table by user ID?"
"Which hash should the URL shortener use?"
"Where does the load balancer go?"

questions.explanation: Step 1 gathers requirements: who uses it, how, how many users, inputs and outputs, data volume, requests per second, and the read to write ratio. Hashing belongs to step 3 (core components). Sharding and load balancers belong to step 4 (scaling), once you know the constraints.

questions.prompt: In your mock you jumped straight to drawing boxes. Explain the four-step flow you will use next time, using "design an agent that answers support tickets" as the example.

model_answer.summary: Scope first, then sketch the high-level design, then detail the core components, then find and fix bottlenecks with their trade-offs. You lead each step.
key_points: Step 1: clarify use cases, constraints and assumptions, such as users, requests per second, data volume and read to write ratio
Step 2: sketch the main components and connections, and justify them
Step 3: design the core components in detail, such as the data model and API
Step 4: identify bottlenecks given the constraints and address them (load balancer, horizontal scaling, caching, sharding), discussing trade-offs

questions.explanation: This is the primer's structure. Its step 4 ends with "Everything is a trade-off", which is what interviewers probe. Writing the step-1 numbers down gives you something to check each later choice against.

questions.prompt: A service gets 10 million requests a day, spread evenly. About how many requests per second is that?

choices.text: About 12
About 116
About 417
About 1,160

questions.explanation: A day has 24 × 60 × 60 = 86,400 seconds, and 10,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 116. Rounding a day to about 100,000 seconds gives a quick 100 per second. Peak traffic is usually higher than the average, so say what peak factor you assume.

questions.prompt: According to the latency numbers in the System Design Primer, about how long is a round trip within the same datacenter?

choices.text: About 500 nanoseconds
About 50 milliseconds
About 5 seconds
About 500 microseconds (0.5 ms)

questions.explanation: The primer's table gives 500,000 ns, which is 500 µs, for a round trip within the same datacenter. For comparison, a main memory reference is about 100 ns and an HDD seek about 10 ms. These orders of magnitude tell you when a network call or a disk read will dominate.

questions.prompt: You add a cache-aside cache in front of the database. Which disadvantage does the System Design Primer list?

choices.text: Cached data goes stale when the database changes; a TTL or write-through helps
The cache writes to the database directly on each update, so writes get slower
Every read still has to go to the database, even when the key is cached
It only works with SQL databases, not with key-value or document stores

questions.explanation: In cache-aside the application reads the cache, and on a miss loads from the database and fills the cache. The cache never talks to the database itself. Its listed downsides are stale data (reduced with a TTL or write-through), three trips on each miss, and an empty cache after a node fails.

questions.prompt: You add more read replicas to handle read load. Which downside does the primer point out?

choices.text: Replicas can take writes, so conflicts appear
The more replicas there are, the more replication lag
Reads can no longer be spread across servers
The primary stops serving reads

questions.explanation: In primary-replica replication the primary takes writes and replicates them to replicas that serve reads. The primer notes that more replicas mean more to replicate and so more replication lag. Heavy writes can also bog replicas down, and data can be lost if the primary fails before replicating. Write conflicts are a primary-primary problem.

questions.prompt: The interviewer says: "Your design now gets ten times more reads." Explain two options and the trade-off of each.

model_answer.summary: Add a cache such as cache-aside, which cuts database reads but risks stale data. Or add read replicas, which add read capacity but bring replication lag and more parts. Scale the stateless app servers horizontally behind a load balancer as well.
key_points: Caching (cache-aside) serves repeated reads from memory and reduces database load
Its trade-off is stale data, reduced with a TTL or write-through, and slower cache misses
Read replicas spread reads across more database servers
Their trade-off is replication lag, extra hardware and complexity
Stateless app servers can scale horizontally behind a load balancer

questions.explanation: All of these are in the primer's scaling step and its caching and replication sections. Naming the trade-off with each option is what the step asks for. Checking the read to write ratio from step 1 tells you whether caching will help at all.

questions.prompt: In the coding mock you can see a brute-force solution and suspect a faster one with a hash map. What should you do before writing code?

choices.text: Code the brute force at once so you have something working, then optimise
Stay quiet and think it through until you are sure of the optimal solution
Outline both approaches and their complexity, then code once the interviewer agrees
Ask the interviewer which data structure to use, so you don't waste time on the wrong one

questions.explanation: The Tech Interview Handbook's checklist says to explain a few approaches at a high level, state their time and space complexity, and only start coding after the interviewer gives the green light. Silence gives the interviewer nothing to assess, and coding the brute force first can use up the time.

questions.prompt: Your code compiles with five minutes left in the mock. Describe what you do in those minutes.

model_answer.summary: Check the code instead of announcing you are done. Scan for mistakes, agree edge cases and step through them, then restate the complexity.
key_points: Scan the code for mistakes such as off-by-one errors
Brainstorm edge cases with the interviewer and add them as test cases
Step through the code by hand with those test cases
Restate the time and space complexity of the final code
Don't announce that you are done straight away

questions.explanation: These are the handbook's after-coding steps. Interviewers score testing and verification, not just a working first draft, so the last minutes count. Write each step you skipped in your stumble list.
